sections.title: Intended use
sections.intro: Where the system is used decides which of the later questions are relevant.

questions.text: In which areas is the system used? Tick all that apply.
questions.help: Questions that cannot apply to these areas are not asked.

options.label: Education or training (schools, universities, vocational training, e-learning)
Recruitment, HR or managing workers
Credit, lending or insurance
Public services or benefits (social security, housing, emergency services)
Healthcare or medical
Recognising or identifying people from their face, voice, fingerprints or other biometric data
Critical infrastructure (energy, water, gas, heating, road traffic, digital infrastructure)
Law enforcement or policing
Migration, asylum or border control
Courts, legal proceedings, elections or referendums
A physical product, or a safety component of one (machinery, toys, vehicles, lifts, medical devices…)
Customer service, marketing, content or internal operations
Something else

sections.title: The company's role
sections.intro: A company can hold more than one role for the same system. Answer for this system only.

questions.text: Does the company develop this AI system (or have it developed) and place it on the market or put it into service under its own name or trademark?
questions.help: Developing covers designing the logic, training the model or building the software. Putting into service includes first use for the company's own purposes.

questions.text: Does the company integrate a third-party AI model into a product or service it offers under its own name?
questions.help: For example a CRM that embeds a third-party API for predictive sales scoring. The company is then the provider of the system, even if not of the model.

questions.text: Does the company put its own name or trademark on an AI system developed by someone else?
Has the company made a substantial modification to an AI system developed by someone else?
questions.help: A change not foreseen by the original provider that affects compliance or the intended purpose, e.g. retraining that changes the system's core outputs.

questions.text: Does the company use or offer the system for a purpose other than the one its provider intended?
questions.help: For example using a general text-summarisation tool to assess creditworthiness.

questions.text: Does the company use this AI system under its authority in a professional capacity?
questions.help: Any use in the course of business, including internal tools. Purely personal use by an individual does not count.

questions.text: Is the system used in the company's own workplace in a way that affects its workers, for example to monitor, evaluate, schedule or allocate work to staff?
questions.help: Workers are the company's own staff. Pupils, customers or members of the public are not workers.

questions.text: Is the company established in the EU and places on the EU market a system bearing the name or trademark of a provider established outside the EU?
Does the company make this system available on the EU market as part of a supply chain, without being its provider or importer (e.g. as a reseller)?
Is the company a body governed by public law, or a private entity providing public services?
questions.help: Relevant to the fundamental rights impact assessment and to registration duties for deployers.

sections.title: Scope exclusions
sections.intro: The AI Act does not apply to some uses at all.

questions.text: Does any of these describe the system's use? Tick all that apply, or none.

options.label: Used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes
Developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development
Research, testing or development before being placed on the market or put into service (not testing in real-world conditions)
Used by a natural person in a purely personal, non-professional activity
Used by a non-EU public authority or international organisation under an international law-enforcement or judicial cooperation agreement

sections.title: Prohibited practices: risk screening
sections.intro: These questions look for signs that the system could fall into a prohibited category. A "yes" is not a finding: it flags the system for the reviewer to assess.

questions.text: Does the system try to change what people decide or do, for example by nudging, persuading or personalising content or offers, in ways they might not notice or fully understand?
Could that influence lead people to decisions they would not otherwise take, in a way that could cause them or others significant harm (financial, physical or psychological)?
Is the system aimed at, or likely to be used by, people who may be easier to influence: children, older people, people with a disability, or people in a difficult social or financial situation?
Could the system take advantage of those circumstances to change their behaviour in a way that could significantly harm them?
Does the system score, rank or rate people over time based on their behaviour or personal characteristics?
Could that score lead to people being treated worse in a context unrelated to where the data was collected, or in a way out of proportion to their behaviour?
Does the system assess or predict how likely a person is to commit an offence?
Does that assessment rely only on profiling or on personality traits, rather than supporting a person's assessment based on objective, verifiable facts linked to a criminal activity?
Can the system generate or edit realistic images, video or audio of people?
Could it produce sexually explicit or intimate content of a real, identifiable person without their consent, or sexual content involving children, without safeguards that reliably prevent this?
Does the system collect facial images in bulk from the internet or from CCTV footage to create or expand a facial recognition database?
Does the system detect or infer people's emotions, mood, stress, attention or intentions from biometric signals such as their face, voice or body movements?
questions.help: Inferences drawn only from what people write are not covered here.

questions.text: Whose emotions or states does it infer? Tick all that apply.

options.label: Employees or other workers, at work
Pupils, students or learners, in education
Other people, for example customers or the public

questions.text: Is it used there solely for medical or safety reasons, for example detecting a driver's fatigue?
Does the system use biometric data (face, voice, fingerprints, gait…) to sort people into groups?
Is that used to deduce or infer people's race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation?
Is the system used by or for law enforcement to identify people at a distance, in real time, in places open to the public?

Is that use limited to searching for specific victims or missing persons, preventing an imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack, or locating suspects of serious crimes, with prior authorisation?

sections.title: High-risk test
sections.intro: A system is high-risk if it is part of a regulated product's safety, or if it is used for one of a set of sensitive purposes.

questions.text: Is the system a safety component of a product, or itself a product, covered by any of this EU product legislation? Tick all that apply, or none.

options.label: Machinery
options.citation: Annex I, Section B, point 21 (moved from Section A by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744)

options.label: Toys
Recreational craft and personal watercraft
Lifts and their safety components
Equipment for potentially explosive atmospheres
Radio equipment
Pressure equipment
Cableway installations
Personal protective equipment
Appliances burning gaseous fuels
Medical devices
In vitro diagnostic medical devices
Civil aviation
Motor vehicles, two- or three-wheel vehicles, agricultural and forestry vehicles
Marine equipment
Rail systems

questions.help: A system used only for user assistance, performance optimisation, efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control is not a safety component, unless its failure or malfunction would endanger health or safety.

questions.text: Does that legislation require the product to undergo a third-party conformity assessment before it is placed on the market or put into service?
questions.help: Answer no if third-party assessment is required only for risks other than health and safety, for example radio spectrum or electromagnetic interference.

questions.text: Is the system intended to be used for any of these purposes? Tick all that apply, or none.

options.label: Biometrics: remote biometric identification (not mere verification of identity)
Biometrics: categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes
Biometrics: emotion recognition
Critical infrastructure: safety component in managing digital infrastructure, road traffic, or water, gas, heating or electricity supply
Education: deciding access or admission to education and training
Education: evaluating learning outcomes
Education: assessing the level of education a person will receive or can access
Education: monitoring prohibited behaviour of students during tests
Employment: recruitment or selection — targeted job ads, filtering applications, evaluating candidates
Employment: decisions on working conditions, promotion or termination, task allocation by behaviour or traits, monitoring and evaluating performance
Essential services: public authorities assessing eligibility for public assistance benefits and services
Essential services: evaluating creditworthiness or establishing a credit score (not fraud detection)
Essential services: risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance
Essential services: evaluating and classifying emergency calls, dispatching emergency services, emergency patient triage
Law enforcement (risk of victimisation, polygraphs, evidence reliability, risk of offending, profiling)
Migration, asylum and border control (polygraphs, risk assessment, examining applications, identification)
Justice: assisting a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and law and applying the law
Democratic processes: influencing the outcome of an election or referendum or voting behaviour

questions.help: Only the purposes that match the areas ticked in Part 1 are listed.

questions.text: Does the system profile natural persons — automated processing of personal data to evaluate aspects of a person's life such as work performance, economic situation, health, preferences, behaviour or location?
Does the system only do one of the following, without materially influencing the outcome of decisions? Tick any that apply, or none.

options.label: Performs a narrow procedural task
Improves the result of a previously completed human activity
Detects decision-making patterns or deviations, and is not meant to replace or influence a completed human assessment without proper human review
Performs a preparatory task to an assessment for one of the purposes ticked above

questions.text: Even if none of the purposes above applies: does the system materially influence a person's access to any of these?
questions.help: This does not make the system high-risk on its own. It flags the system for the reviewer, because the list of high-risk uses can be extended.

options.label: Employment
Finance (loans, credit, insurance)
Healthcare
Education
Essential public services (social security, housing)
Legal or administrative decisions

sections.title: Transparency duties
sections.intro: These apply whatever the risk class.

questions.text: Is the system intended to interact directly with natural persons (e.g. a chatbot or voice assistant)?
Does the system generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content?
Does the company use the system to generate or manipulate image, audio or video content that is a deep fake?
Does the company publish AI-generated or manipulated text to inform the public on matters of public interest, without human editorial review?

rules.rationale: The company develops the system and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name, so it is the provider.
The company integrates a third-party model into a product it offers under its own name, so it is the provider of the resulting system (and a downstream provider of the model).

Putting its own name or trademark on a system developed by someone else makes the company the provider. Art. 25(1) is written for high-risk systems; for other systems the reviewer should confirm the company also meets the Art. 3(3) definition.
A substantial modification makes the company the provider of the modified system; the original provider is generally no longer responsible for it.
Changing the intended purpose of the system makes the company its provider where the system becomes high-risk as a result.
The company uses the system under its authority in a professional capacity, so it is a deployer.
The company places on the EU market a system bearing the name of a provider established outside the EU, so it is an importer.
The company makes the system available in the supply chain without being its provider or importer, so it is a distributor.

The company is both the provider and a deployer of the system. As provider it writes the instructions for use itself (Art. 13), so using the system in line with them (Art. 26(1)) is treated as met through its provider duties and is not listed as a separate obligation.
The system is used at the company's own workplace and affects its workers, so the duty to inform workers and their representatives applies if the system is high-risk.

add.attention: No AI Act role was identified for this system. Check whether the company has any relationship to it that the questionnaire missed.

rules.rationale: None of the role tests applied. Without a role, no obligations attach to the company for this system.
The company is a body governed by public law or a private entity providing public services.
Systems used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes are outside the AI Act.
Systems developed and put into service solely for scientific research and development are outside the AI Act.
Research, testing and development before a system is placed on the market or put into service is outside the AI Act (testing in real-world conditions is not).
Deployers who are natural persons using AI in a purely personal, non-professional activity are outside the AI Act's deployer obligations.
Use by non-EU public authorities or international organisations under international cooperation agreements is outside the AI Act, subject to adequate safeguards.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(a): assess the system against it before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system influences people's decisions in ways they may not notice and could cause significant harm. This points to a risk of manipulative or deceptive techniques prohibited by Art. 5(1)(a). This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(b): assess the system against it before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system could take advantage of people's age, disability or social or economic situation in a way that harms them. This points to a risk of exploiting vulnerabilities, prohibited by Art. 5(1)(b). This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(c): assess the system against it before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system scores people over time and the score could lead to unjustified or disproportionate detrimental treatment. This points to a risk of social scoring, prohibited by Art. 5(1)(c). This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(d): assess the system against it before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system predicts the risk of a person offending based only on profiling or personality traits. This points to a risk of a practice prohibited by Art. 5(1)(d). This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(e): assess the system against it before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system collects facial images in bulk from the internet or CCTV to build a facial recognition database. This points to a risk of untargeted scraping, prohibited by Art. 5(1)(e). This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(f): assess the system against it before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system infers the emotions of workers or learners from biometric data, other than for medical or safety reasons. This points to a risk of emotion recognition in the workplace or in education, prohibited by Art. 5(1)(f). This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(g): assess the system against it before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system uses biometric data to infer sensitive characteristics. This points to a risk of biometric categorisation prohibited by Art. 5(1)(g). This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(h): assess the system against it before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system is used for real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement outside the narrow exceptions. This points to a risk of a practice prohibited by Art. 5(1)(h). This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Possible prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(ba)–(bb): check the intended purpose and the safeguards against misuse (Art. 5(1a)) before confirming the classification.

rules.rationale: The system could generate non-consensual intimate content of identifiable people, or sexual content involving children, without safeguards that reliably prevent it. This points to a risk of a practice prohibited from 2 December 2026. This is a risk flag, not a finding: the reviewer must assess it before confirming the classification.

add.attention: Real-time remote biometric identification relies on the Art. 5(1)(h) exceptions: check the authorisation and safeguards of Art. 5(2)–(7).

rules.rationale: The company states that real-time remote biometric identification is limited to the exceptions in Art. 5(1)(h), which require prior authorisation and safeguards.
The system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I legislation that requires third-party conformity assessment, so it is high-risk.

add.attention: High-risk under Art. 6(1) through Annex I, Section B legislation: the AI Act's high-risk requirements apply through that sectoral legislation (Art. 2(2)), not as separate obligations here. Check the sectoral requirements.

rules.citation: Art. 6(1), Art. 2(2), Annex I, Section B, as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744
rules.rationale: The system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product under Annex I, Section B legislation (civil aviation, vehicles, marine equipment, rail or, since the Digital Omnibus, machinery) that requires third-party conformity assessment. It is high-risk, but for these products only Art. 6(1), Art. 60a and Arts. 102–112 of the AI Act apply; the high-risk requirements reach the product through the sectoral legislation.

add.attention: Covered by Annex I legislation but without third-party conformity assessment: not high-risk under Art. 6(1). Confirm the conformity route under the sectoral law.

rules.rationale: The product is covered by Annex I legislation but does not require third-party conformity assessment, so Art. 6(1) does not make it high-risk.
The system's intended purpose is listed in Annex III, so it is high-risk unless the Art. 6(3) derogation applies.
Creditworthiness evaluation.
Life and health insurance pricing.
The system profiles natural persons, so the Art. 6(3) derogation cannot apply: an Annex III system that profiles is always high-risk.

The system only performs a task listed in Art. 6(3) and does not profile, so it is not high-risk despite the Annex III use case. A provider relying on this must document the assessment (Art. 6(4)) and register the system (Art. 49(2)).
The Art. 6(3) derogation only concerns Annex III. The system remains high-risk under Art. 6(1).

add.attention: Not listed in Annex III, but the system influences access to rights or essential services. Reviewer should check the Annex III wording closely and watch for Commission amendments under Art. 7.

rules.rationale: The system influences access to rights or essential services without matching an Annex III point. This does not make it high-risk, but it is flagged for the reviewer.
The system interacts directly with natural persons, so they must be informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious.
The system generates synthetic audio, image, video or text, so its outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated.
The system performs emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, so people exposed to it must be informed.
The company uses the system to produce deep fakes, so it must disclose that the content was artificially generated or manipulated.
The company publishes AI-generated text on matters of public interest without human editorial review, so it must disclose that the text was artificially generated.
Transparency duties apply, so the system is in the limited-risk category.
The system is high-risk.
High-risk through Annex I, Section B legislation.
The screening points to a risk of a prohibited practice.
The system is outside the scope of the AI Act.
No prohibited practice, high-risk use case or transparency duty applies. The system is minimal-risk: only AI literacy (Art. 4) applies, and voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged (Art. 95).
